author: npew
text: Pre-train hierarchical policy (coarse + fine levels) with supervised learning on demonstrations, then fine-tune using RL. Hierarchy enables tasks with many steps. Neat that you can also get away with sparse rewards (and do better), signaling a future without reward shaping!

quoted.text:
New paper -  RelayPL

Takeaway: Goal conditioned hierarchical policy when infused with unstructured play data and a relabelling trick can solve REALLY LONG horizon tasks!

author: npew
text: @andrey_kurenkov The perception is still far from perfect, and solving it would take as much effort again. Contacts are hard to model, and hand degrades in perf over time. But the policy learns to deal with all of this. So I suspect traditional approaches would be tricky.

author: npew
text: @themitak @OpenAI thank you! giraffe has been watching our progress for a while now, and keeps us honest by literally pushing the limits :)

author: npew
text: @OpenAI In the end, this result is not so much about the Rubik's Cube, as it is about learning dexterity as step towards general purpose robots. The techniques are quite general: RL + ADR could in principle be applied to any task you can simulate.

author: npew
text: @OpenAI Another surprising side-effect of using ADR with a recurrent neural network, was the emergence of meta-learning. Our hypothesis is that the network learns to both solve the task and figure out the properties of the environment it's in (the real world) at the same time. 8/n

author: npew
text: @OpenAI One anecdote was that during the filming, one of the fingers of the robot broke, but we didn't notice for over an hour since the robot still kept solving the cube. 7/n

author: npew
text: @OpenAI The network is also surprisingly robust. We messed with the robot quite a bit: occluding cameras, put on a rubber glove, tied the fingers. And it still does a fairly solid job at solving the cube. 6/n

author: npew
text: @OpenAI The strategies the neural network policy learns are often suprising, but once you see them make a lot of sense. For example, the hand uses its little finger much more than a human, but its little finger is also abnormally big. 5/n

author: npew
text: @OpenAI For example, modeling friction of cubelets, springiness, etc would be really hard to figure out best randomizations for. 4/n

author: npew
text: @OpenAI This lead us to automatic domain randomization (ADR). ADR removed a ton of manual work to set randomizations, which would have been super tricky with Rubik's cube. 3/n

author: npew
text: @OpenAI It's been suprising to me how well sim2real works with RL + domain randomization. The biggest obstacle we faced was to set randomization ranges as complexity of the environment increased. 2/n

author: npew
text: Excited to share what we've been working on at @OpenAI Robotics for the past year: we used RL and a new technique called automatic domain randomization to train a robot to solve Rubik's Cube. 1/n

quoted.text:
We've trained an AI system to solve the Rubik's Cube with a human-like robot hand.

This is an unprecedented level of dexterity for a robot, and is hard even for humans to do.

The system trains in an imperfect simulation and quickly adapts to reality: https://t.co/O04izt3KvO https://t.co/8lGhU2pPck

author: npew
text: My happiness grows with every new protected bike lane in SF!

quoted.text: The 5th St Safety Project just passed the SFMTA Board, which will bring protected bike lanes & pedestrian safety improvements to the high-injury corridor! While the long-term changes are being made, our quick-build policy will allow for short-term safety measures immediately.
